subject: Communication
title: How Misinformation Spreads Online
description: A short lesson to help you apply How Misinformation Spreads Online.

hook.text: MIT found that false news spreads six times faster than true news on Twitter.

buildup.text: Vosoughi, Roy, and Aral analyzed 126,000 stories spread by 3 million people.

discovery.text: Humans share misinformation because it triggers strong emotions — outrage, fear, surprise — that demand sharing.

twist.text: Bots helped, but humans were the main spreaders. We don't need AI to spread lies — our psychology does it naturally.

climax.text: Algorithms amplify what gets engagement. Misinformation gets more engagement. The system rewards falsehood by design.

punchline.text: Lies spread fast because they feel important. Truth is often boring.

quiz.question: How much faster does false news spread compared to true news, according to MIT research?

details.summary: Misinformation spreads faster than truth online because it is more novel and emotionally arousing. MIT research found false news reaches 1,500 people six times faster than accurate stories. Social sharing, algorithmic amplification, and emotional engagement drive viral misinformation.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the mechanics of misinformation spread is essential for recognizing and resisting false narratives before they shape your beliefs.
takeaways: False news spreads six times faster than accurate news
Novelty and emotional arousal drive sharing behavior
Algorithms amplify engaging content regardless of accuracy

faq.question: Why does misinformation spread faster than truth?
faq.answer: False information tends to be more novel and emotionally provocative, triggering stronger sharing impulses. True information is often nuanced and less dramatic. Social media algorithms reward engagement, not accuracy, so emotionally charged false content gets amplified more than careful reporting.

faq.question: Can technology solve the misinformation problem?
faq.answer: Technology can help but cannot solve it alone. Fact-checking algorithms catch some false content but struggle with context and nuance. Platform design changes can reduce viral spread.
